questions.q: Fill up: Puerperium = up to ______; fourth trimester = up to 12 weeks.
opts: 6 weeks : 12 weeks
12 weeks : 6 weeks
4 weeks : 8 weeks
8 weeks : 12 weeks
questions.exp: Puerperium = up to 6 weeks; fourth trimester = up to 12 weeks. (Book p567)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about Definitions, postnatal visits & uterine involution is TRUE?
opts: ACOG: an initial visit at 3 weeks and a final visit at 12 weeks — GOI: day 1, day 3, day 7 and 6 weeks
ACOG: day 1 and 6 weeks only — GOI: visits at 3 weeks and 12 weeks
ACOG: visits at 2, 4 and 6 weeks — GOI: day 1, day 7 and day 42
ACOG: a single visit on day 7 — GOI: a single visit at 6 weeks
questions.exp: ACOG restructures postnatal care as an ongoing process with a contact by 3 weeks and a comprehensive visit by 12 weeks; India schedules four early visits. (Book p567)

questions.q: All of the following are Definitions, postnatal visits & uterine involution EXCEPT:
opts: Just below the umbilicus; 20 weeks; cricket ball; 1000 g
At the xiphisternum; 36 weeks; football; 2000 g
At the symphysis; 12 weeks; tennis ball; 500 g
Midway to symphysis; 16 weeks; orange; 300 g
questions.exp: Just below umbilicus (≈20 wks), cricket-ball consistency, 1000 g; after 24 h fundal height falls 1.25 cm/day. (Book p567)

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman at 2 weeks with definitions, postnatal visits & uterine involution presents with the uterus halves to about 500 g in a week, is impalpable by two weeks at about 300 g, and completes. Uterine weight – after 1 week : 2 weeks : 4 weeks; and position at 1 and 2 weeks?
opts: About 500 g at one week, 300 g at two weeks and 100 g by four weeks
About 300 g at one week, 100 g at two weeks and 50 g by four weeks
About 750 g at one week, 500 g at two weeks and 300 g by four weeks
About 1000 g at one week, 500 g at two weeks and 100 g by four weeks
questions.exp: The uterus halves to about 500 g in a week, is impalpable by two weeks at about 300 g, and completes involution at 100 g by four weeks. (Book p567)

questions.q: Fill up: Involution = ______ size (not number), faster in nulliparous; USG normal by 8 weeks.
opts: ↓ muscle cell size; nulliparous; 8 weeks
↓ muscle cell number; multiparous; 4 weeks
Apoptosis; breastfeeding; 2 weeks
Fibrosis; nulliparous; 12 weeks
questions.exp: Involution = ↓ muscle size (not number), faster in nulliparous; USG normal by 8 weeks. (Book p567)

questions.q: Fill up: The puerperium lasts about ______ weeks, and the uterus becomes a pelvic organ again at about ______ days after delivery.
questions.exp: The fundus descends roughly 1 cm a day and is no longer felt abdominally by about 10-14 days, with involution complete by six weeks. (Book p567)

questions.sec: Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
questions.q: Which of the following statements about Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function is TRUE?
opts: Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function — The isthmus; 2–3 cm
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function — The fundus; 5 cm
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function — The vagina; 1 cm
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function — Obliterated; 4 cm
questions.exp: LUS → isthmus; cervix 10 cm → 2–3 cm for few days → closes. (Book p568)

questions.sec: Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
questions.q: All of the following are Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function EXCEPT:
opts: Pin-point : transverse slit-like — Nulliparous pin-point; multiparous transverse slit
Transverse slit : pin-point — Nulliparous pin-point; multiparous transverse slit
Round : stellate — Nulliparous pin-point; multiparous transverse slit
Slit : round — Nulliparous pin-point; multiparous transverse slit
questions.exp: Nulliparous pin-point; multiparous transverse slit. (Book p568)

questions.sec: Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
questions.q: A 28-year-old woman at 7 weeks with cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function presents with uterine artery doppler in the puerperium shows increased vascular resistance throughout the first 7 . Uterine artery Doppler in the puerperium shows:?
opts: Raised vascular resistance throughout the first 7 weeks post-partum
Reduced vascular resistance for 6 months after delivery
Absent diastolic flow for the first 24 hours after delivery
No change at all from the antepartum Doppler findings
questions.exp: Uterine artery Doppler in the puerperium shows increased vascular resistance throughout the first 7 weeks post-partum. (Book p568)

questions.sec: Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
questions.q: Fill up: Lochia (superficial decidual sloughing) components and sequence ______.
opts: Decidua, blood, leucocytes and exudate; rubra, then serosa, then alba over 24-36 days
Blood alone; ten days of rubra followed by twenty days of alba
Mucus and pus; alba first, then serosa, then rubra
Amniotic fluid, lasting seven days in total after the delivery
questions.exp: Lochia is decidua, blood, leucocytes and serous exudate, passing through rubra, serosa and alba over roughly 24-36 days. (Book p568)

questions.sec: Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
questions.q: Which of the following statements about Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function regarding 6 weeks; endometriosis; palm-size to 3–4 is TRUE?
opts: 6 weeks; endometriosis; palm-size to 3–4 cm after 2 weeks
2 weeks; infection; 10 cm to 1 cm
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function — 12 weeks; polyp; fist to 5 cm
Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function — 1 week; fibroid; palm to 8 cm
questions.exp: Placental site: 6 weeks; m/c site for endometriosis; palm-size → 3–4 cm by 2 weeks. (Book p568)

questions.sec: Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
questions.q: In partially/non-breastfeeding women – menstruation returns by ______; ovulation by ______ (earliest ______).
opts: 6–8 weeks; 7 weeks (5–11 weeks); 28 days
12 weeks; 10 weeks; 6 weeks
4 weeks; 2 weeks; 14 days
6 months; 3 months; 8 weeks
questions.exp: Menses 6–8 wks; ovulation ~7 wks (5–11), earliest 28 days. (Book p568)

questions.sec: Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
questions.q: Match the lochia with its timing and appearance — 1) Lochia rubra 2) Lochia serosa 3) Lochia alba … A) Red, containing blood, shreds of decidua and membranes, for the first three or four days B) Pinkish or brownish serous discharge from about day four to day ten C) Pale or yellowish white discharge continuing for several weeks after that
questions.exp: Rubra then serosa then alba is the normal sequence; offensive or persistently red lochia suggests endometritis or retained products. (Book p568)

questions.sec: Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
questions.q: Contraception in the puerperium – non-breastfeeding : breastfeeding.
opts: Non-breastfeeding: combined pills avoided for 21 days — breastfeeding: progestogen-only before an intrauterine device
Combined pills are preferred in both groups from the first postpartum day
An intrauterine device only for non-breastfeeding women, and nothing at all for breastfeeding women
Injectable progestogen only for non-breastfeeding women, and combined pills for breastfeeding women
questions.exp: Combined pills are avoided for 21 days because of thrombosis risk and they reduce milk supply; progestogen-only methods suit breastfeeding. (Book p569)

questions.sec: Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
questions.q: Lactational amenorrhoea – mechanism and failure rate:
opts: ↑ prolactin inhibits GnRH → ↓ LH and FSH; pregnancy risk 4% per year
↑ oxytocin inhibits FSH; 10% per year
↓ estrogen; 1% per year
↑ progesterone; 0.5% per year
questions.exp: Prolactin → GnRH inhibition → ↓ LH/FSH; 4% failure per year. (Book p569)

questions.sec: Haematological, renal & other puerperal changes; after-pains
questions.q: Blood parameters after delivery include all EXCEPT:
opts: Marked lymphocytosis
Marked leucocytosis (≤25,000/µL) with ↑ granulocytes, relative lymphopenia, absolute eosinopenia
Marked thrombocytosis and high fibrinogen in 1st week
↓ Hb and hematocrit
questions.exp: Leucocytosis up to 25,000, granulocytosis, relative lymphopenia, eosinopenia, thrombocytosis, high fibrinogen, ↓ Hb/Hct. (Book p569)

questions.sec: Haematological, renal & other puerperal changes; after-pains
questions.q: Other parameters after delivery:
opts: Weight loss of 5-6 kg at birth, then 2-3 kg from diuresis, with a very high cardiac output for 24-48 hours
Polyuria with a weight gain of 2 kg and hypokalaemia from rapid sodium retention
An immediate weight loss of 10 kg with a persistently low cardiac output for two days
Oliguria with hypernatraemia and a falling fibrinogen from postpartum coagulopathy
questions.exp: Blood loss and diuresis account for early weight loss, and the cardiac output stays very high for one to two days, which matters in heart disease. (Book p569)

questions.sec: Haematological, renal & other puerperal changes; after-pains
questions.q: Time for parameters to return to normal – blood volume : CO & HR : GFR : dilated ureter/renal pelvis.
opts: 1 week : 10 days : 2 weeks : 2–8 weeks
10 days : 1 week : 6 weeks : 2 weeks
2 weeks : 2 weeks : 1 week : 12 weeks
6 weeks : 6 weeks : 6 weeks : 6 weeks
questions.exp: Blood volume 1 wk; CO/HR 10 d; GFR 2 wks; ureter/pelvis 2–8 wks. (Book p569)

questions.sec: Haematological, renal & other puerperal changes; after-pains
questions.q: After-pains are:
opts: Seen in multiparous women; oxytocin-driven contractions worse with suckling, settling by day 3
Seen in primiparous women; prostaglandin-driven, persisting for two weeks
Caused by retained placental fragments and needing uterine curettage
Caused by infected lochia and treated with a course of antibiotics
questions.exp: After-pains are intermittent oxytocin-driven contractions, commoner in multiparas, aggravated by breastfeeding and settling by the third day. (Book p569)

questions.sec: Haematological, renal & other puerperal changes; after-pains
questions.q: Which of the following statements about normal puerperal changes is TRUE?
opts: The leucocytosis of labour settles within about a week and after-pains are commoner in multiparous women
Haemoglobin falls steadily for six weeks because the red cell mass keeps shrinking
After-pains are commoner in primigravidas than in multiparous women
The raised blood urea of pregnancy persists for at least six weeks after delivery
questions.exp: After-pains are worse in multiparas and during breastfeeding; the leucocytosis settles and haemoglobin stabilises once haemodilution resolves. (Book p569)

questions.q: Causes of subinvolution of uterus (m/c first):
opts: Retained placental fragments are commonest, then infection and incompletely remodelled vessels
Infection is commonest, with uterine fibroids the next most frequent cause
Anaemia is commonest, and breastfeeding delays involution further
Multiparity is commonest, with maternal obesity the next cause
questions.exp: Retained products are the commonest cause; breastfeeding releases oxytocin and actually helps the uterus to involute. (Book p570)

questions.q: Clinical features of subinvolution:
opts: Excessive or prolonged bleeding with a uterus larger than expected for the postpartum day
Amenorrhoea with a small, well-involuted uterus on bimanual examination
High fever with a closed cervical os and no lochia being passed at all
A painless white discharge with itching and no abnormal bleeding
questions.exp: Subinvolution presents as prolonged or excessive lochia with a uterus that is bigger and softer than it should be for the day. (Book p570)

questions.q: IOC is pelvic USG – findings for retained products : incompletely remodelled spiral artery.
opts: Retained products: a thick vascular endometrium — remodelling: tubular hypoechoic areas in the myometrium
Retained products: a thin endometrium — remodelling: a uniformly small uterus
Retained products: free fluid in the pouch — remodelling: an adnexal mass
Retained products: an empty cavity — remodelling: a thick endometrium
questions.exp: Retained products show as a thickened vascular endometrium, while a remodelling defect shows tubular hypoechoic spaces in the myometrium. (Book p570)

questions.q: Management of subinvolution and the caution:
opts: A uterotonic first, then gentle curettage; vigorous curettage risks Asherman syndrome
Immediate hysterectomy, since a uterus that has failed to involute never recovers
Antibiotics alone, because subinvolution is always caused by occult endometritis
Methotrexate to dissolve the retained trophoblast, then a repeat scan in two weeks
questions.exp: A uterotonic is the drug of choice, with gentle curettage for suspected retained tissue; over-zealous curettage causes intrauterine adhesions. (Book p570)

questions.q: All of the following predispose to subinvolution of the uterus EXCEPT:
opts: Exclusive breastfeeding with regular suckling
Retained products of conception
Pelvic infection or endometritis
Uterine fibroids or a retroverted uterus
questions.exp: Breastfeeding releases oxytocin and actually promotes involution; retained tissue, infection and fibroids delay it. (Book p570)

questions.q: Prolactin peaks in the ______ and ______ after delivery; milk production is ______-dependent with the first stimulus being ______.
opts: Third trimester; falls; prolactin; ↓ estrogen after placental delivery
First trimester; rises; oxytocin; suckling
Second trimester; falls; estrogen; ↑ progesterone
At delivery; rises; oxytocin; ↓ prolactin
questions.exp: Prolactin highest in 3rd trimester, falls after delivery; production prolactin-dependent, triggered by ↓ estrogen; ejection is oxytocin-dependent. (Book p570)

questions.q: Colostrum contains more of everything than mature milk EXCEPT (mnemonic KFC):
opts: K+, fat, carbohydrates & Ca2+
Protein, IgA, vitamin A
Sodium, chloride, zinc
Lactoferrin, lysozyme
questions.exp: Colostrum is poorer in K+, fat, carbohydrate and calcium. (Book p570)

questions.q: Absolute contraindication to breastfeeding:
opts: Galactosemia or lactose intolerance in the baby
Maternal HIV infection in the Indian setting
Mastitis affecting one breast in the puerperium
COVID-19 infection in the mother after delivery
questions.exp: The absolute contraindication to breastfeeding listed is galactosemia or lactose intolerance in the baby. (Book p571)

questions.q: Relative contraindications to breastfeeding:
opts: Intravenous drug abuse, an active herpes lesion on the breast and untreated pulmonary tuberculosis
Maternal HIV infection, hepatitis B carriage and recent COVID-19 infection
Mastitis, a breast abscess and engorgement in the first postpartum week
Iron deficiency anaemia, gestational diabetes and treated hypothyroidism
questions.exp: Breastfeeding is encouraged in HIV on treatment, hepatitis B and mastitis; intravenous drug abuse, herpetic breast lesions and untreated TB are contraindications. (Book p571)

questions.q: Which are NOT contraindications to breastfeeding?
opts: HIV on treatment, COVID-19, mastitis, and hepatitis B positivity once the baby is immunised
Classic galactosaemia in the infant, which is an absolute contraindication
Untreated active pulmonary tuberculosis in the mother
An active herpes lesion on the breast itself
questions.exp: Breastfeeding continues in treated HIV, COVID-19 and mastitis, and in hepatitis B carriers once the infant has received immunoglobulin and vaccine. (Book p571)

questions.q: Fill up: Milk ejection or the let-down reflex is mediated by ______ released in response to suckling, whereas milk synthesis depends mainly on ______.
opts: oxytocin; prolactin
prolactin; oxytocin
oestrogen; progesterone
human placental lactogen; oxytocin
questions.exp: Prolactin drives synthesis and oxytocin drives ejection; this is why breastfeeding causes after-pains and helps uterine involution. (Book p571)

questions.sec: Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
questions.q: Postpartum endometritis – m/c site and risk factors:
opts: The placental site, after caesarean section, chorioamnionitis or prolonged rupture of membranes
The cervix, particularly after an operative vaginal delivery at term
The uterine fundus, after a short and uncomplicated labour
The cornua, which are the most exposed areas in a twin pregnancy
questions.exp: Infection begins at the raw placental site; caesarean, chorioamnionitis and prolonged rupture are the principal risk factors. (Book p571)

questions.sec: Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
questions.q: Presentation and management of postpartum endometritis:
opts: Fever, subinvolution and uterine tenderness with offensive lochia; broad-spectrum antibiotics
Painless bleeding with a well-involuted uterus; evacuation of retained products
Profound shock with a flaccid uterus; emergency hysterectomy
Secondary amenorrhoea with hot flushes; hormonal replacement therapy
questions.exp: Endometritis presents with postpartum pyrexia, a tender poorly involuted uterus and offensive lochia, and is treated with antibiotics. (Book p571)

questions.sec: Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
questions.q: Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis – vessel, P/V finding, blood culture, imaging:
opts: Ovarian vein, right more than left; cord-like structure; culture negative; MRI or CT
Uterine vein; a fluctuant mass on palpation; culture positive; ultrasound
Iliac artery; a pulsatile mass on palpation; culture positive; Doppler
Renal vein; nothing palpable on examination; culture negative; plain X-ray
questions.exp: Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis affects the ovarian vein (right more than left), shows a cord-like structure on P/V, has a negative blood culture because the infection is localized, and MRI or CT may show the thrombosed vein. (Book p571)

questions.sec: Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
questions.q: Key clinical features of septic pelvic thrombophlebitis:
opts: Broad-spectrum antibiotics have no effect; clinical diagnosis
Responds promptly to antibiotics
Diagnosed by blood culture
Presents with PPH
questions.exp: Persistent fever despite BSA; clinical diagnosis. (Book p571)

questions.sec: Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
questions.q: On the fourth day after a caesarean section a woman develops a fever of 38.8 C with uterine tenderness and offensive lochia. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
opts: Postpartum endometritis — broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering aerobic and anaerobic organisms
Normal puerperal changes — reassurance and no treatment
A urinary tract infection — oral antibiotics alone
Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis — immediate anticoagulation alone
questions.exp: Fever with uterine tenderness and offensive lochia after caesarean is endometritis, treated with intravenous clindamycin and gentamicin or equivalent. (Book p571)

questions.sec: Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
questions.q: Management of septic pelvic thrombophlebitis – no thrombophlebitis evidence : evidence of thrombophlebitis.
opts: No evidence: continue BSA and LMWH; evidence: heparin for 6 weeks
No evidence: stop all antibiotics; evidence: warfarin for 3 months
No evidence: heparin for 6 weeks; evidence: heparin for 48 hours
No evidence: surgery to ligate the vein; evidence: antibiotics only
questions.exp: Without evidence of thrombophlebitis, continue broad-spectrum antibiotics and LMWH, with heparin until 48 hours after the woman is afebrile; with evidence of thrombophlebitis, give heparin for 6 weeks. (Book p572)

questions.sec: Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
questions.q: Fever in a breastfeeding woman due to breast engorgement is characterised by:
opts: Rarely ≥39 °C and lasts <24 hours
Always >40 °C for a week
Associated with rigors and pus
Persists until weaning
questions.exp: Engorgement fever rarely ≥39 °C, lasts <24 h. (Book p572)

questions.q: Burning, numbness and tingling over the upper outer thigh/lateral hip after vaginal delivery indicates injury to:
opts: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, which is the nerve most often injured
The femoral nerve, compressed against the pelvic brim by the fetal head
The common peroneal nerve, compressed at the neck of the fibula
The obturator nerve, stretched by the descending head in the cavity
questions.exp: Meralgia paraesthetica is entrapment of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh under the inguinal ligament in labour. (Book p572)

questions.q: Quadriceps weakness sparing adductors with sensory loss over anterior and medial thigh indicates:
opts: Femoral nerve injury (2nd m/c)
Obturator nerve injury
Sciatic nerve injury
Pudendal nerve injury
questions.exp: Femoral nerve – 2nd m/c; adductors spared. (Book p572)

questions.q: Foot drop after delivery is due to ______ injury from ______.
opts: The common peroneal nerve, from prolonged squatting or pressure in the leg supports
The tibial nerve, injured by prolonged positioning in lithotomy
The sciatic nerve, injured by the epidural needle during analgesia
The femoral nerve, compressed by the forceps blades at delivery
questions.exp: Foot drop follows compression of the common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck, classically from squatting or leg supports. (Book p572)

questions.q: M/c nerves injured after caesarean section:
opts: Ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves
Femoral and obturator
Pudendal and sciatic
Genitofemoral and lateral cutaneous
questions.exp: Post-CS: ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves. (Book p572)

questions.q: Match the nerve injury with its clinical picture — 1) Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh 2) Femoral nerve 3) Common peroneal nerve … A) Foot drop and loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot after prolonged lithotomy or squatting B) Burning pain and numbness over the outer thigh from compression at the inguinal ligament C) Weakness of knee extension with a depressed knee jerk from compression against the pelvic brim
questions.exp: Meralgia paraesthetica, femoral neuropathy from the retractor or fetal head, and peroneal palsy from leg supports or squatting are the classic injuries. (Book p572)

units.title: Definitions, postnatal visits & uterine involution
units.guide: Separate puerperium from the fourth trimester, schedule ACOG and GOI postnatal visits, and chart the uterus shrinking week by week. Focus for this checkpoint: Definitions, postnatal visits & uterine involution.

units.title: Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function
units.guide: Track the lower segment, cervix and os, sequence the lochia, time placental-site healing and return of ovulation in breast- and non-breastfeeding women. Focus for this checkpoint: Cervix, lochia, placental site & ovarian function.

units.title: Haematological, renal & other puerperal changes; after-pains
units.guide: Recall the blood-count and fluid shifts after delivery, when each parameter normalises, and the nature of after-pains. Focus for this checkpoint: Haematological, renal & other puerperal changes; after-pains.

units.title: Subinvolution of the uterus
units.guide: Identify the m/c cause of subinvolution, its clinical features, USG findings and the uterotonic-then-curettage management. Focus for this checkpoint: Subinvolution of the uterus.

units.title: Breastfeeding: hormones, colostrum & contraindications
units.guide: Distinguish prolactin from oxytocin roles, what colostrum lacks, and which maternal conditions truly contraindicate breastfeeding. Focus for this checkpoint: Breastfeeding: hormones, colostrum & contraindications.

units.title: Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis
units.guide: Diagnose postpartum endometritis by site and risk factors, recognise septic pelvic thrombophlebitis clinically and manage with heparin for the correct duration. Focus for this checkpoint: Puerperal pathologies: endometritis & septic pelvic thrombophlebitis.

units.title: Obstetric neuropathy
units.guide: Match burning thigh, quadriceps weakness and foot drop to the injured nerve and its mechanism, and know the nerves most often injured after caesarean. Focus for this checkpoint: Obstetric neuropathy.
